levels.title: New to GitHub
levels.who: You have never used GitHub, or you've only followed a link to it. You don't need to write code.
levels.aim: Understand what GitHub is, read a project's page with confidence, and use this catalogue to find code that matters to your work.
steps: Learn the five words that matter: repository, README, commit, issue and organisation. The list below explains each in a sentence.
Search this catalogue in everyday words, such as 'benefits' or 'school data'. Results are grouped and explained in plain English.
search
Open a project's profile. Start with the summary at the top: what it does, who it belongs to and whether it's still looked after.
profile
See who a project belongs to, from the GitHub account up to the government department.
family
Look anything up in the plain-English guide when a word is new.
glossary
When you're ready, follow GitHub's Hello World exercise below. It takes about 15 minutes and you can't break anything.
words: Repository (repo)
A folder for one project: its files, its history and the conversation about it.
README
The front page of a repository. It should say what the project is, who it's for and how to use it.
Commit
A saved change, with a note saying what changed and who changed it. The history of commits is how you can trace any change.
Issue
A note on a repository to report a problem, ask a question or suggest an idea.
Organisation (account)
A shared GitHub account for a team or department, which owns its repositories.
Public and private
Anyone can see a public repository. Only invited people can see a private one; this catalogue only covers public code.
Archived
Read-only. The project is kept for reference but is no longer changed.

levels.title: Intermediate
levels.who: You can find your way around a repository and want to judge a project, contribute to one or look after your own.
levels.aim: Judge whether a project is well looked after, take part through issues and pull requests, and know what good looks like in government.
steps: Check how well a project is looked after: README, licence, code owners, recent activity and automated checks.
practice
Compare a project with the GDS Way and the Service Manual's guidance on open code.
gdsway
Find projects that publish a website with GitHub Pages, and who runs them.
pages
Explore projects by topic and by organisation to find work you could reuse rather than rebuild.
topics
Raise an issue or propose a change with a pull request, following the GitHub flow.
Use the analytics dashboard to see patterns across the estate.
insights
words: Branch
A separate line of work, so changes can be made and reviewed without affecting the main version.
Pull request
A proposal to merge a branch's changes, with review and discussion before they go in.
Fork
Your own copy of someone else's repository, used to propose changes when you can't change theirs directly.
CODEOWNERS
A file naming who must review changes to which parts of a repository.
Licence
Says how others may use the code. Government code is usually MIT; content is usually under the Open Government Licence.
GitHub Pages
A website published straight from a repository.

levels.title: Advanced
levels.who: You run repositories, organisations or migrations, or build on this catalogue's data.
levels.aim: Secure and automate repositories, plan moves between organisations without breaking anything, and reuse the catalogue's data and feeds.
steps: Review the security and supply-chain signals: secret scanning, Dependabot, pinned actions and branch rules.
safe
Plan a move between organisations: the migration plan, the checks before and after, and what breaks on transfer.
plan
Find legacy technology and technical debt by organisation, with the evidence behind each signal.
legacy
Reuse the data: download feeds, the knowledge graph (SKOS, OWL, PROV) and the DCAT catalogue.
knowledge
Trace every requirement to the checks that prove it, and every defect to its fix.
trace
Link straight into the catalogue: #repo=<account>/<repository>, #org=<GOV.UK slug>, #legacy=<GOV.UK slug>, #account=<GitHub account>.
words: GitHub Actions
Automated workflows that run on events such as a push or pull request: tests, builds, deployments.
Rulesets and branch protection
Rules for what may be merged and by whom, such as required reviews and checks.
Secret scanning and push protection
Finds credentials committed to a repository and can block them before they are pushed.
Dependabot
Raises alerts and pull requests for vulnerable or out-of-date dependencies.
Transfer
Moving a repository to another account. GitHub redirects old links, but Pages, packages and some settings need extra steps.
REST API
The programmable interface to GitHub, used for audits, inventories and automation.
